title: Boston dumps Flock, says it shared data nationwide in violation of contract
gist: Boston abandoned Flock Safety's license-plate readers after a vendor-side 'error' exposed Boston Police camera data to a nationwide police lookup despite contractual sharing being disabled, but the city immediately moved on to trials with Motorola (Feb 2026) and Axon (June 2026) — the loss is vendor-specific, not category-wide. Flock claims new city partnerships are outpacing nonrenewals roughly 10 to 1 in 2026 even as EFF documents officers logging search justifications like 'LOL' and 'sexy'.

insights.claim: Boston's 45-camera Flock Safety license-plate-reader pilot leaked Boston Police data to other law enforcement agencies nationwide within three days of launch because Flock enabled a nationwide lookup feature despite the contract requiring data sharing to be disabled and BPD confirming the settings were off.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A configuration default that overrides a signed contract term is a product-liability and procurement-risk vector for the whole surveillance-camera category, not a one-off bug.
insights.quote: Within three days of initiating the Pilot, BPD became aware that other law enforcement agencies were able to access license plate and vehicle information collected from BPD ALPR cameras using a nationwide lookup feature that was enabled by the vendor in error.

insights.claim: Boston's annual surveillance technology report never disclosed how many outside law enforcement agencies actually accessed the improperly shared license-plate data, leaving the breach's real scope unquantified.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Undisclosed exposure scope keeps tail liability open; later disclosure could reignite the story and municipal contract reviews.
insights.quote: The report didn’t say how many law enforcement agencies accessed the data.
insights.locator: The report didn’t say how many

insights.claim: Boston replaced Flock with competing license-plate-reader trials — Motorola starting February 2026 and Axon starting June 2026 — showing that municipal ALPR budgets rotate between vendors rather than disappearing when one vendor fails a privacy test.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Flock-specific headline risk is a share-shift opportunity for Motorola and Axon rather than a shrinking TAM for surveillance hardware.
insights.quote: The police department started another license-plate reader trial with Motorola in February 2026 and a third trial with Axon in June 2026.

insights.claim: Boston Mayor Michelle Wu set a procurement standard that disqualifies any surveillance platform whose access controls can be silently reset by the vendor, making configuration-integrity guarantees a competitive requirement for camera vendors.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Vendors that can prove tamper-evident, contractually-bound access controls will win the next wave of municipal RFPs; those that cannot get dropped mid-pilot.
insights.quote: When the toggles or the access controls either are not able to be restricted in the ways that conform with that policy, or are set but then can be unset or reset in ways that violate that policy, we would not use that platform.
insights.locator: It can really help with safety in a lot of ways

insights.claim: Boston requires license-plate-reader vendors to contractually agree not to share data and to erase recordings after 30 days unless police request retention for legal or investigative purposes, a template other cities can copy directly.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Short mandated retention windows cap the data-asset value vendors can build from municipal deployments, pressuring data-monetization business models.

insights.claim: An Electronic Frontier Foundation analysis of Flock Safety search logs found officers across the country accessing sensitive location data while logging justifications such as 'LOL,' 'LMAO,' 'sexy,' and 'idk,' documenting systemic misuse rather than isolated incidents.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Concrete log evidence is the kind of exhibit that drives legislation and class actions, escalating regulatory risk beyond reputational noise.
insights.quote: Police are routinely searching the Flock database without providing any legitimate justification, making a mockery of our civil liberties by logging reasons like ‘LOL’
insights.locator: An EFF analysis of ALPR search logs

insights.claim: Flock Safety's remediation — a dropdown list of crimes officers must pick before searching, in place since late 2025 — does not require any proof that the selected reason matches the search's true purpose, so the audit trail remains unverifiable.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A compliance control that cannot be audited will not satisfy regulators, implying further product rework or mandated logging costs ahead.
insights.quote: does not require proof that the dropdown reason actually matches the true purpose of the search

insights.claim: Flock Safety told Ars that so far in 2026 new city partnerships have outpaced nonrenewals by roughly 10 to 1, a company-supplied metric that directly contradicts reporting that cities are dropping the company at an accelerating pace.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Watch whether net-new logo growth holds against churn headlines — the 10-to-1 claim is unaudited and is the key number to pressure-test on any Flock financing or secondary.
insights.quote: so far in 2026, new city partnerships have outpaced nonrenewals by approximately 10 to 1

insights.claim: Cities are dropping Flock over a stacked set of reasons — out-of-control surveillance, unwanted data sharing, high expenses, and police abuse of the tool — meaning cost, not only privacy, is part of the churn driver.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: If pricing is a co-driver of churn, cheaper Motorola or Axon bundles can take share even if privacy rules never tighten.
insights.quote: over concerns regarding out-of-control surveillance, unwanted data sharing, high expenses, and reports of police abusing the tool
